blocks.text: **The problem.** Given a string `s` and a list of words `wordDict`, return `true` if `s` can be cut into a sequence of one or more dictionary words. A word may be used any number of times.

blocks.alt: s equals applepenapple, with the dictionary apple and pen. Under the letters is the dp row, one cell for each cut position from 0 to 13. dp[0] is true for the empty prefix. dp[5] is true because apple follows it, dp[8] because pen follows dp[5], and dp[13], the whole string, because apple follows dp[8]. Every other cell is false.

elements.text: dp[i] is T when a T cell j is followed by a word s[j..i)
elements.originalText: dp[i] is T when a T cell j is followed by a word s[j..i)

blocks.code:
s = "leetcode",       wordDict = ["leet", "code"]                    ->  true   ("leet code")
s = "applepenapple",  wordDict = ["apple", "pen"]                    ->  true   ("apple pen apple")
s = "catsandog",      wordDict = ["cats", "dog", "sand", "and", "cat"] ->  false

blocks.text: Cutting the string one word at a time and trying every word is a search with many repeated questions: in `"catsandog"`, both `"cats" + "and"` and `"cat" + "sand"` end up asking whether `"og"` can be split. So ask the question once per **prefix** instead.

The first i letters can be split exactly when some **shorter prefix can be split** and the letters after it, `s[j..i)`, form **one word**. That's a one-string DP: `dp[i]` for the first i letters, with `dp[0] = true` (the empty prefix needs no words) and the answer in `dp[n]`. The last word is at most as long as the longest dictionary word, L, so only the last L cut points need checking.

**Time O(2ⁿ) in the worst case, space O(n)** for the call stack. With `s = "aaaa…ab"` and the words `"a"`, `"aa"`, `"aaa"`, every way of cutting up the a's is tried before the b makes each one fail. Remembering the answer for each `start` (memoisation) fixes it — and that is exactly the table below, filled from the other end.

blocks.caption: dp[i] is true when some true dp[j] is followed by a dictionary word s[j..i).

blocks.code:
def word_break(s, word_dict):
    words = set(word_dict)
    longest = max(len(w) for w in word_dict)
    # dp[i]: can the first i letters, s[:i], be split into dictionary words?
    dp = [False] * (len(s) + 1)
    dp[0] = True                          # the empty prefix needs no words
    for i in range(1, len(s) + 1):
        for j in range(max(0, i - longest), i):
            if dp[j] and s[j:i] in words:     # a good split up to j, then one word
                dp[i] = True
                break
    return dp[len(s)]

blocks.text: **Time O(n · L²), space O(n + D),** where L is the longest word and D the total size of the dictionary. Each of the n prefixes tries at most L cut points, and each try slices and hashes up to L letters.

blocks.alt: Try each word next: O(2^n) time, O(n) space. DP over prefixes: O(n·L²) time, O(n + D) space.

blocks.text: The DP is the expected answer. Explaining *why* recursion is slow — the same suffix asked about again and again — is what shows you understand why DP is the right tool.

items: **Greedy fails** — `"goalspecial"` with `["go", "goal", "goals", "special"]`: taking the longest word first, `"goals"`, leaves `"pecial"`; the DP finds `"goal" + "special"`.
**Almost works** — `"catsandog"` splits up to `"og"` and no further: false.
**The whole string is one word** — `dp[n]` comes straight from `dp[0]`.
**Forgetting `dp[0] = true`** — then nothing can ever be true.
**Word Break II** — return every split, not just whether one exists: backtracking, with the dp row (or a memo) to skip dead ends.
**Decode Ways** — count the ways to cut a digit string into codes from 1 to 26: the same prefix DP, adding counts instead of OR-ing booleans.
**Concatenated Words** — which words in a list are built from other words in the list? A word break check for each one.
**Edit Distance** — back to two strings and a 2D table, with three moves at every cell. Next lesson.
